bio.en: David Placek is the founder of Lexicon Branding, the firm that pioneered the discipline of brand naming and created iconic names including BlackBerry, Pentium, Swiffer, and the Impossible Burger.
bio.zh: David Placek 是 Lexicon Branding 的创始人，该公司开创了品牌命名这门行当，并创造了包括 BlackBerry、Pentium、Swiffer 和 Impossible Burger 在内的标志性名称。

summary.en: A great brand name outlasts every other element of a company, so it deserves serious investment rather than a last-minute afterthought. Placek's team deliberately seeks names that provoke tension and polarization within a client's team, because comfort with a name usually signals it is not distinctive enough. He breaks the naming process into three steps—identify, invent, implement—and relies on small creative teams, linguists, and a proprietary "sound symbolism" engine rather than big brainstorms. For founders without those resources, he recommends a simple "diamond" exercise focused on behavior and experience, generating 1,000-plus directions without judging them, and choosing a bold name you won't immediately love. He also stresses that the .com is no longer critical and that the right name creates asymmetric and cumulative advantage in the market.
summary.zh: 一个伟大的品牌名比公司的其他一切元素都更长久，所以它值得认真投入，而不是临上线前才草草了事。普拉塞克的团队会刻意寻找能在客户团队内部引发张力和两极分化的名字，因为对一个名字感到舒服，通常意味着它不够独特。他把命名流程拆成三步——识别、发明、落地——依靠的是小创意团队、语言学家，以及一套专有的"语音象征"引擎，而非大型头脑风暴。对于没有这些资源的创始人，他建议做一个简单的"菱形"练习，聚焦行为和体验，先生成上千个方向、先别评判，最后选一个大胆、你不会一眼爱上的名字。他还强调 .com 已不再关键，而对的名字能在市场上带来不对称优势和累积优势。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Your brand name, nothing's going to be used more often or for longer than that name. Design will change, messaging will change, products will change, but that name is there.
turns.zh: 你的品牌名，没有什么比它用得更频繁、用得更久的了。设计会变，文案会变，产品会变，但那个名字一直都在。

turns.speaker: David Placek

turns.zh: 我们追求的是分歧。我们想看到团队为了一个名字争得面红耳赤。这种两极分化，恰恰说明这个名字有力量。大多数客户来做命名项目时，都信心满满地以为"一看就知道对不对"，但事实是，这种情况几乎从未发生。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: The story I like to tell is a story of Sonos. One, a great client team. I worked with all the founders. But at the time, they were stuck on being in a brand name that put them in the entertainment business. And so when we presented Sonos, which has many qualities to it, it was rejected because it doesn't have enough emotion to it. It's not entertainment-like. And we argued about that because I said, "This is outside looking in, but I don't see you as an entertainment company. You make speakers that allow for the flow of entertainment through these things. And Sonos is about sound." But it had a particular quality. It's called a palindrome, which really means that you can flip it and it means the same thing. In the case of Sonos, you could also turn it upside down and it was essentially the same. (00:06:47): And so that got them thinking about this, but they were still has... So I left that meeting in Santa Barbara, and I came back and they were still struggling with it. And I got on a plane, didn't even bill them for this, went back down to Santa Barbara and met with them again and said, "I really believe in this name and I think it's the right for you." And at a certain point, one of the founders, Bob MacFarlane, who's just a wonderful client. I could see him thinking, and he said, "You know? We're trying to name this for ourselves, and what we really should be doing is naming it for the marketplace and the customers. And I think Sonos now is the right name. And I felt really good about that." He later wrote me a note about how I help to do that, and we use it sometimes in credentials presentations because it's such a nice note. (00:07:45): But Sonos is something I'm so glad that I had this internal energy to, "I got to go down there and make a bid for this." I don't do that often, by the way, but I felt very strongly about Sonos.
turns.zh: 我最爱讲的故事是 Sonos 的故事。首先，这是个很棒的客团队，我和所有创始人都共事过。但当时他们卡在一点上：他们想用一个能把自己塞进"娱乐行业"的名字。所以当我们提交 Sonos 的时候——这个名字其实有很多优点——它被否决了，理由是它不够有情感、不够"娱乐感"。我们为此争论，因为我说："这是从外面看进去的视角，但我不觉得你们是一家娱乐公司。你们做的是音箱，让娱乐通过这些设备流动起来。而 Sonos 关乎的是声音。"不过它有个特别之处：它叫回文词，意思是你把它反过来，意思还是一样。放到 Sonos 上，你把它倒过来看，也基本是一样的。（00:06:47）这让他们开始思考，但他们还是有点……所以那次在圣巴巴拉的会议结束后我离开了，回来之后他们还在纠结。于是我直接上了飞机——连差旅费都没让他们出——又飞回圣巴巴拉，再次跟他们会面，说："我真的相信这个名字，我觉得它适合你们。"后来在某个时刻，其中一位创始人 Bob MacFarlane——他真是位好客户——我能看出他在琢磨，然后他说："你知道吗？我们一直在为'自己'取名字，可我们真正该做的，是为市场和客户取名字。我觉得现在 Sonos 就是对的名字。"我听了特别欣慰。后来他还给我写了张便条，讲我怎么帮了他们，我们有时会在展示案例时拿出来用，因为那张便条写得太好了。（00:07:45）但 Sonos 这件事，我很庆幸自己当时有那股劲——"我得下去为这个名字争取一下"。顺便说一句，我不常这么干，但我对 Sonos 的感觉特别强烈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love Sonos. I love the name. I have many Sonos products. How often does this happen where the client is just, "No, this is not the name. We have this bigger vision, we have a whole other idea of it." And then you convince them.
turns.zh: 我喜欢 Sonos。我喜欢这个名字。我有很多 Sonos 的产品。这种事经常发生吗——客户直接说"不，这不是我们要的名字，我们有更大的愿景，我们对它有完全不同的想象"，然后你把他们说服了？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Well, it happens all of the time. And it's a little bit bidirectional, right? Most clients, and I can understand this, they come to a naming project absolutely believing, with full confidence, that they're going to know it when they see it. And the truth is, it almost never happens. I think this year we'll hit 4,000 projects that we've completed. (00:08:37): And it's interesting, we'll tell people in a very polite way, "You're not going to know when you see it." But I know they don't believe me. And even when... You could see them thinking that, "You know what? He was right. I really have to think about this. I have to process it." And part of that, part of why clients don't like the bolder names, the more imaginative names that we present is they are looking for comfort. And that's the opposite that what you want to do. And part of our job here is to help people to give the confidence that going bolder, and bigger, and being uncomfortable. I use the expression, "There is no power in comfort, not in the marketplace."
turns.zh: 嗯，这种事一直都在发生，而且有点双向的意思，对吧？我能理解，大多数客户来做命名项目时，都百分之百确信自己"看到就知道对不对"。可事实是，几乎从来不是这样。我想今年我们完成的命名项目会达到 4000 个。（00:08:37）有意思的是，我们会很客气地告诉客户："你看到的时候是不会知道的。"但我知道他们压根不信。甚至等到……你能看出他们在想："你知道吗？他说得对。我真的得好好想想，我得消化一下。"客户不喜欢我们提交的那些更大胆、更有想象力的名字，一部分原因就是他们在寻求"舒服"。而你想要的恰恰相反。我们的工作之一，就是帮人们建立信心，去更大胆、更放飞、去拥抱不舒服。我用一句话来总结："舒适里没有力量，至少在市场上没有。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. There's so much here already. So this idea of you're not going to know it when you see it is something that people come in with thinking like, "Once I see it, it'll be obvious." Just why is that almost never the case? Is it because the name has to be something that is uncomfortable?
turns.zh: 哇，信息量已经很大了。所以"看到的时候你不会知道"这个观点，其实人们带着"我一看到肯定就一目了然"的预期来的。为什么几乎总不是这样？是因为好名字必须让人不舒服吗？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: There's a lot of psychology to this, which ironically, I never even took a psychology class in college or graduate school. But the first element is humans do like to be comfortable. And one of the mechanisms of comfort is if something's been successful before, then I feel like I can approve it or select it. This is why movies like Harry Potter or even novels like Jack London's Call of the Wild get rejected so many times. I think Harry Potter was rejected 16 or 18 times, and Jack London's book even more than that. I mean, think about it. He's pitching a book and they say, "What are you talking about here? You're saying a dog becomes a wolf? I've never heard of anything like that." So, we really do have to help people think about, "It's not about the past. You're actually creating the future." And we really talk to people and emphasize the idea, "This isn't a name you're creating. We're creating an experience for you. We're going to work together." (00:10:54): And our conversations always start with, "Talk to us about how you behave now and how you want to behave in the future," as opposed to, "Tell me about your positioning, tell me about your values, tell me about your mission." That's really kind of old thinking. It's very traditional, and that did work 25 or 30 years ago. But this is a far more complex, interconnected world, a digital world now that stuff just doesn't create... It doesn't create names like Sonos or some of our other credentials that we probably will talk about today.
turns.zh: 这背后有很深的心理学，讽刺的是，我大学和研究生的心理学课一堂都没上过。但第一点是：人确实喜欢舒服。而"舒服"的机制之一就是——如果某样东西以前成功过，我就会觉得"这我能认可、能选"。这就是为什么像《哈利·波特》这样的电影，甚至像杰克·伦敦的《野性的呼唤》这样的小说，会被拒绝那么多次。我记得《哈利·波特》被拒了十六七次，杰克·伦敦那本书被拒得更多。你想想，他拿一本书去推销，人家说："你这说的是什么？你说一只狗变成狼？我从来没听过这种东西。"所以我们真的得帮人们换个念头："这不是关于过去，你其实是在创造未来。"我们跟人聊的时候，会反复强调一个想法："你不是在创造一个名字，我们是在为你创造一种体验，我们要一起干。"（00:10:54）我们的对话永远从这句话开始："跟我们说说，你们现在是怎么做的，未来想怎么做"，而不是"跟我说说你的定位、你的价值观、你的使命"。那套是老思想，很传统，二三十年前确实管用。但现在的世界复杂得多、互联得多，是个数字世界，那种老办法根本造不出……造不出像 Sonos，或我们今天大概会聊到的其他那些经典名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we're going to talk about just the process you guys go through, so stay tuned for that. But before we get to that, is there's another story you can share that shows this idea of being bold?
turns.zh: 好，你们的具体流程我们待会儿再聊，先卖个关子。不过在那之前，你还能不能再讲一个故事，体现这种"大胆"？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: I'll talk about Microsoft's Azure. So when Microsoft came to us, they were pretty much stuck. And Microsoft does... And in many ways, to their credit, a lot of things don't need to be named. They don't need trademarks. They don't need brand names. They need descriptors. And so they came to us to develop a name that started or ended with cloud. Made sense to them because it was a cloud service. And our reaction was, "If you do that, you're going to be in an ocean of other cloud this, cloud that. And you have an opportunity as Microsoft here to really emerge as a leader in this." And so, there was a discussion about, "Okay, we'll take a look at those, but we'd like to see some cloud names." Which is easy to do, by the way.
turns.zh: 我讲讲微软的 Azure 吧。微软来找我们的时候，其实挺卡住的。说实话，平心而论，微软很多东西根本不需要取名字——不需要商标，不需要品牌名，它们只是一些描述词。所以他们来找我们，是想做一个以 cloud 开头或结尾的名字。对他们来说这很合理，因为那就是云服务嘛。我们的反应是："如果你们这么做，就会淹没在一大片 cloud 这个、cloud 那个的海洋里。而作为微软，你们明明有机会真正脱颖而出，成为这一领域的领导者。"于是就有了这样的讨论："行，那些我们也会看看，但我们还是想看一些带 cloud 的名字。"——说句实话，那种名字最容易做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Classic.
turns.zh: 经典。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: So, we did that. And along the way, we came up with this word azure, which is another word for blue. And so there was a link to clouds, blue sky clouds, things like that, but we really presented it based on its linguistic qualities. It's a noisy word, that Z in there. It starts with an A, and it ends in a nice smooth flow. So, we really strive to do create names that are balanced. And in a very busy competitive world, having a strong signal, which is generated by noise is a good thing. (00:13:27): The reaction wasn't good. One of the clients said, "That's just a dumb idea." Remarks like that. At this point, after these four decades, it just rolls off my back like water off a duck is what my grandmother would say. But I think along the way, as we talked about it, they began to warm up to this. And now of course it's, I don't know, a $100 billion brand or something like that. But that's an example of, "I haven't seen that before. I'm very comfortable with cloud. Cloud is what it is. We're describing it." But that's a statement. And I think that... Well, I don't think I know that's what I said in one of the presentations is, "You don't want to make a statement here. You want to start a story." And Azure is going to behave differently in the marketplace than Cloud Pro, which is I think one of the names that we presented to them on the other site at their request.
turns.zh: 于是我们就照做了。过程中我们想出了 azure 这个词，意思是"天蓝色"。所以它和云、蓝天白云能扯上关系，但我们真正打动客户的是它的语言学特质。这是个"吵"的词，里面有那个 Z。它以 A 开头，结尾又收得很顺滑。所以我们的目标，一直是造出平衡的名字。在竞争极其激烈的世界里，有个由"噪音"带来的强信号，是好事。（00:13:27）但当时的反应并不好。有个客户说："这主意简直蠢透了。"类似的话不少。走到今天这四十年了，这些话就像我奶奶说的，从我背上滑下去，像水从鸭子身上滑落一样，根本不往心里去。不过我觉得，聊着聊着，他们开始接受它了。现在它当然是——我不知道——价值上千亿美金的品牌了吧。但这正好说明那个问题："我以前没见过这个，我对 cloud 很舒服，cloud 就是它本来的样子，我们只是在描述它。"可那只是在"下结论"。我记得在某一场提案里我说过："你在这里不该下结论，你该开启一个故事。"Azure 在市场上的表现，会和 Cloud Pro 完全不同——Cloud Pro 好像是我们应他们要求、在另一边给他们提的名字之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad they went with Azure. Let me actually ask this question. I know you're biased, but just how important is a great name? If you had a better name than a product that was better than you, does that make a big difference? Just anything you can share there to help people see this is the power of a great name.
turns.zh: 我很高兴他们最后选了 Azure。我想认真问个问题。我知道你肯定有偏向，但一个好名字到底有多重要？如果一个名字比你更好的产品，本身却比你还弱，那名字能造成很大差别吗？随便分享点什么，帮大家看清好名字的威力。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Let's look just at the reality of this. Your brand name, whether it's a product name or a company name, nothing's going to be used more often or for longer than that name. Design will change, messaging will change, products will change, but that name is there. So, I like to talk about this idea of cumulative advantage. Over time, as people buy more and more of the product, they see it more often, that their bond between you and that brand, or them and the brand I should say, becomes stronger and stronger. So you want that name to stick in their mind to be distinctive, because distinctiveness is what creates that cumulative advantage. (00:15:35): The second thing is this notion of what I call asymmetric advantage. It makes perfect sense, and most clients agree with this when we say this is that even before you launch this brand, why not start with an advantage in the marketplace? And you won't get an advantage if you're descriptive. If you are Cloud Pro and there's 10 other cloud services, you're not going to stand out in the marketplace. You won't have the ability to create necessarily that cumulative advantage in the marketplace. (00:16:09): So, those are my two reasons why names are, I think, done right. And we do talk about our mission is not creating good names. A lot of people can do that. Our mission is to create the right name for clients, because the right name does deliver asymmetric advantage and cumulative advantage for you. And that, for us, has almost unlimited value.
turns.zh: 我们就看现实吧。你的品牌名，不管是产品名还是公司名，没有什么比它用得更频繁、更长久的了。设计会变，文案会变，产品会变，但那个名字一直都在。所以我喜欢讲一个概念：累积优势。随着时间推移，人们买的产品越来越多、看到这个名字的次数越来越多，你和那个品牌之间——或者说他们和品牌之间——的联结就越来越强。所以你希望这个名字能在他们脑子里扎下根、有辨识度，因为正是辨识度造就了累积优势。（00:15:35）第二点是我想说的"不对称优势"。这很好理解，我们这么讲的时候大多数客户都认同：既然如此，为什么不在品牌还没发布之前，就先在市场里占个优势？而你如果用的是描述性名字，就得不到这个优势。如果你是 Cloud Pro，而市面上还有十个别的云服务，你在市场里根本冒不出来，也就未必能建立起那种累积优势。（00:16:09）这就是我认为"名字取对了"的两个理由。我们也常说，我们的使命不是创造"好名字"——那很多人都能做。我们的使命是给客户创造"对的名字"，因为对的名字能为你带来不对称优势和累积优势。对我们来说，这几乎有无穷的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a great answer. Essentially what you're saying is it's not going to necessarily make or break you, but it gives you an advantage. A great name gives you an advantage, especially if you're just getting started. You need every advantage you can get.
turns.zh: 这个回答太好了。说白了就是：名字不一定能决定你的生死，但它能给你优势。一个好名字能给你优势，尤其是你刚开始的时候——你能拿到的每个优势都至关重要。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Exactly. And this is maybe a little bit off a tangent, but one of the best books on marketing I've ever read, which is not a book on marketing, and you may have read it along the way in college if you studied any Greek or classics. It's called the Melian Dialogues. And it's a dialogue... It'll take anybody listening to this maybe 25 minutes to read it. Between the Athenians and the government of Melos, the Athenians had decided that they needed that island. And they went and approached them very nice way, that, "We want to take over the island. Nothing will change. You'll be taxed a little bit, but we'll protect you." And the Athenians had thought every aspect about how to take that island before. So by the time they got there, they had created asymmetric advantage in terms of ships, and men, and all of this other stuff. (00:17:57): By the way, in the book, there's no mention of marketing or brand strategy or any of these things, but if you read it, you begin to see that it's marketing, really, is about a symmetric advantage. And so, why not start from the very beginning with an advantage? That's the value of a name.
turns.zh: 没错。这可能有点跑题，但我读过最好的营销书，其实不是一本营销书——如果你大学学过希腊语或古典学，可能途中读过。它叫《米洛斯对话录》。这是一段对话……任何人听这期，花 25 分钟就能读完。对话发生在雅典人和米洛斯岛的政府之间，雅典人已经决定要拿下那个岛。他们过去跟对方很客气地说："我们想接管这个岛。什么都不会变，你们就交点税，但我们会保护你们。"而雅典人早在动手之前，就已经把拿下那个岛的方方面面都谋划好了。所以等他们到那儿时，已经在船只、兵力，还有其他所有东西上，建立了不对称优势。（00:17:57）顺便说一句，这本书里压根没提营销、品牌战略之类的词，但你读的时候会慢慢发现，营销本质上讲的就是不对称优势。既然如此，为什么不一开始就带着优势出发呢？这就是名字的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's dive into the actual process you guys go through, and I want to read a quote that Guillermo Rauch shared when I asked him about what it was like working with you. He's the CEO and co-founder of Vercel, which you guys worked with. I definitely want to hear that story, by the way. So he said, "Before David, the ability to name something was like charisma. You either have it or you don't. It was so surreal to watch his team distill it down to a science." (00:18:35): So let me just ask you, what does that science look like? What are the steps to coming up with an amazing name for your product or company that you guys go through?
turns.zh: 我们深入聊聊你们实际走的流程吧。我想先念一段 Guillermo Rauch 说的话——我当时问他跟你合作是什么体验，他分享的。他是 Vercel 的 CEO 兼联合创始人，你们帮他家取过名。说真的，那个故事我一定要听。他是这么说的："在认识 David 之前，取名字这件事就像个人魅力，要么有要么没有。看着他的团队把它提炼成一套科学，真的太超现实了。"（00:18:35）那我就直接问你：这套科学长什么样？你们给产品或公司想出一个绝妙名字，都要经过哪些步骤？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: That's very nice of Guillermo. He is a very impressive innovator in this category and we greatly enjoyed working with him. Well, our process is real. I break it down in three steps. First, we have to identify, then we invent, and then we implement. It's just three things. It's not rocket science, but it's a combination of creativity and discipline. And obviously, talented people and experience in these things. So, let's just go through those things. In the first section of identify, it's really trying to find out from the client, let's talk about behavior. So, how are you behaving now and how do you want to behave in the future? That behavior is bidirectional. In other words, the marketplace behaves towards a Vercel, that's the name we created for Guillermo. And they behave towards the marketplace. And that's an important point because everything... Buildings are bidirectional. Look at a building, you behave differently towards a temple than you or a church versus a Holiday Inn in terms of how that architecture states. So, we focus on that. Behavior is closely aligned for us with experience. How do you want the experience of this brand? (00:20:11): Now, when we listen to those things, we begin to think about rhythm of the name. So something like Dasani has a lot of rhythm to it, right? It's kind of calming. And so, we'll begin to extract things from that discussion on experience. We will then, also, as part of this first phase, look at the competition. We call that developing a landscape. And we're looking for what are the words... What are the brand names, first, and then what language are they using in this space? Because we have to be distinctive. If a brand name isn't distinctive, you lose. Then, you're imitating. And that's a form of suicide. That's a famous quote from some... I think the president of P&G 50 years ago or something like that. So, that's that first phase which allows us to create what we call a creative framework. And we don't even use the word objectives here because that gets too logical. (00:21:16): Actually, framework for us is a metaphor for a window for us, and our teams, and our linguists to travel through. To open things up so that we're not coming back with a narrow list of names. We're coming back with names that have depth, and breadth, and have different experiences and personalities to them. And clients will sign off on that. And then, we get going. So now, we're moved to the invent stage. (00:21:44): And in the invent stage, we do really two things. You can look at this as two layers of our process. I think the second layer is probably what makes us quite unique in the marketplace. It's the result of millions of dollars of R&D on our part. So the first thing is, no surprise to anyone, we work with creative individuals. And we don't use... This will be contrary. We don't use large brainstorming sections. I did. When I first started the company, I used freelancers, I used large brainstorming groups. And along the way through some analysis, we really discovered that that was not really working for us. That actually, the names were coming from employees and from small groups. And so we've moved our process to, at least, two or three small teams of two people. (00:22:41): And each of those teams... So let's say on significant projects, we always use three teams. And each team gets a different briefing. One team knows everything about the project but the other teams don't. If we're working for Microsoft, the second team thinks they're working for Apple. I mean, they know it's disguised. We're not keeping this from anyone. And then the third team, we take it out of computers, and they might be naming a bicycle or a car or something like that. What we're trying to do is open up the coffers of creativity for this. And so when people are working on what they know is not the real assignment, they are now free to make all kinds of mistakes. And so, most of our names have come out of the second or third team because they're-
turns.zh: Guillermo 过奖了。他是这个领域非常了不起的创新者，我们和他合作得很愉快。我们的流程是实打实的。我把它拆成三步：先识别（identify），再发明（invent），最后落地（implement）。就这三件事。不是什么火箭科学，但它是创造力和纪律的结合，当然也离不开有才华的人和经验。我们逐一过一遍。识别阶段，核心是从客户那里挖出东西——我们来聊聊"行为"。你们现在是怎么做的，未来想怎么做？这个行为是双向的。换句话说，市场对 Vercel——就是我给 Guillermo 造的那个名字——有它的行为方式，而他们也对市场有行为方式。这点很重要，因为万事万物……建筑也是双向的。你看一栋建筑，面对神庙、面对教堂，和面对一家假日酒店，你的行为方式是完全不同的，取决于它的建筑语言在"说"什么。所以我们聚焦在这一点上。行为对我们来说，和"体验"紧密相连。你希望这个品牌给人什么体验？（00:20:11）听完这些，我们就会开始琢磨名字的节奏感。像 Dasani 这个名字节奏感就很强，对吧？让人觉得挺 calming 的。所以我们会从关于体验的讨论里提炼东西。然后，在识别阶段，我们也会去看竞争对手。我们叫它"绘制版图"。我们要找的是这片领域里用的都是什么词、都是些什么品牌名，然后他们用的是什么样的语言？因为我们必须有辨识度。如果一个品牌名没有辨识度，你就输了，那等于在模仿，而模仿是一种自杀——这是某位……我想是五六十年前宝洁总裁的名言。所以这就是第一阶段，它让我们可以搭建出一个我们所谓的"创意框架"。我们甚至不用"目标"这个词，因为那太逻辑化了。（00:21:16）其实对我们来说，框架就像一扇窗，我们的团队和语言学家可以穿过去。把空间打开，这样我们带回来的就不是一份很窄的名字清单，而是一批有深度、有广度、带有不同体验和个性的名字。客户会在这上面签字确认，然后我们才正式开工。下一步就进入"发明"阶段。（00:21:44）发明阶段，我们其实做两件事，你可以把它看作两层。我觉得第二层大概是我们能在市场上独树一帜的原因，那是我们在研发上投了几百万美元换来的。第一件事毫不意外：我们和创意人员合作。而且我们不用——这点可能反直觉——我们不用大型头脑风暴。我以前用过。刚创业时，我雇自由职业者、搞大型头脑风暴小组。但后来通过一些分析，我们发现那对我们根本不奏效。真正出名字的，其实是员工和小团队。所以我们把流程改成了至少两三个两人小队。（00:22:41）每一个小队……在重要项目上，我们永远用三个队，而且每个队拿到的简报都不一样。一个队知道项目的一切，其他队不知道。如果我们在给微软干活，第二个队会以为自己在给苹果干活——当然他们知道这是伪装，我们没瞒着谁。第三个队，我们干脆把项目从电脑里抽离出来，让他们去给一辆自行车或一辆车取名字什么的。我们想做的，是打开创造力的金库。所以当人们知道自己做的不是真正的任务时，他们反而敢放开手脚犯各种错。我们大多数名字，恰恰就是从第二或第三个队里冒出来的，因为他们……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah. I think the process, at some point, I will hopefully write either a good article on this or maybe even a book. But this process would work for, I think, a lot of things. I know it would. All right now, what's that second layer that I talked about? Well, we have made significant investments in this area of linguistics and cognitive science, and it's in two ways. One, building proprietary knowledge. So we know through research that we funded, an extensive amount about an area in language called or linguistics called the sound symbolism. So, what are the sounds of the 26 letters of the alphabet and what do they do? How do they evoke things? Well, it turns out that each of those letters sends out a signal that creates a certain sort of vibration, if you will, or experience. (00:24:31): Now, there's been research on that over the years but there were some gaps, and we decided to fill this. And over the years, we've had a very good relationship with Stanford University, with their Department of Linguistics. We've hired linguists from MIT, from Berkeley. We have a linguistic internship here. I actually just ran this number, preparing for this discussion. We have employed, over four decades now, 253 linguists. Most of them PhDs, some of them contracts, some of them actual employees. That's a lot of intellectual knowledge. So we really have, what I call, a linguistic engine here. And then we now have an operating network of... I just checked on this figure yesterday. We have 108 linguists in 76 countries that help us. Some of them do creative work, others will do just the analysis of names for us. So now, we have that creative framework, we have creative teams working on this. (00:25:39): Now, we're tapping into databases that have over 18,000 small word units, technically called morphemes. So, we also can tap in from a sound standpoint. What are the sounds of reliability? What are the sounds of aliveness? And so with Sonos, by the way, we wanted things that are somewhat noisy. And so S is a noisy letter, like a Z or even a V. And so, you begin to set priorities about what letters we're going to use. And that work from that, we call it an engineering layer floats up into the creative teams. And so, it's a mixture of things at a certain point in time. (00:26:27): All right. Now, what happens to all that? At a certain point, usually 3 to 4 weeks into this, we might have 2 or 3,000 ideas. I say ideas because they're not all solutions, they're not all workable. They may be just beginning ideas, concepts. And we sift through those. And now one of the major challenges that we face, and certainly our clients face, is the need to clear a trademark for it to be not in conflict with a marketplace that is... We're almost reaching a tipping point in terms of difficulty of clearing names here. And so we have paralegals here, and we have a trademark attorney, and we'll analyze those names. That gets us to a much smaller set. And then, we'll do our linguistic work with our linguists, and we end up with a set of names to show our clients. (00:27:22): We'll do this twice with most assignments. Sometimes, we'll do just one time depending on timing and budget. But we really try to get two cycles here, partly because humans love to compare. If you're looking for a house, you don't just look at the first house and say, "Okay, let's sign us up." You look and you learn that we don't need a swimming pool, but we do need a view. It's the same with names. And so, we get feedback from our clients. And sometimes, that's a co-creative process where a client will come up with a word or a solution and we'll then run that through our screening mechanisms for them. And that's really the process. The final phase is implementing.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得这套流程，将来某个时候我希望能写篇好文章，甚至写本书。而且我相信这套流程对很多事都管用，我知道它管用。好，回到我说的第二层。我们在语言学和认知科学这块投了不少钱，方式有两种。一是建立专有知识。通过我们自己资助的研究，我们对语言里一个叫"语音象征"（sound symbolism）的领域了解得非常深。也就是：字母表 26 个字母各自的声音是什么、它们能做什么、它们怎么唤起某种感受？结果发现，每个字母都会发出一个信号，制造出某种震动感，或者说某种体验。（00:24:31）多年来这方面一直有研究，但有些空白，我们决定把它补上。这些年我们和斯坦福大学语言学系关系很好，也从 MIT、伯克利招语言学家，这里还有语言学实习项目。为了准备这次对话，我刚算了下这个数：四十年来，我们雇佣过的语言学家有 253 位。大多数有博士学位，有些是合同工，有些是正式员工。这是大量的知识积累。所以我说我们这里有一台真正的"语言学引擎"。另外我们现在还有一张运营网络——我昨天刚核过这个数——在 76 个国家有 108 位语言学家帮我们，有的做创意，有的专门帮我们做名字分析。所以现在我们有了创意框架，有了创意团队在跑。（00:25:39）我们还接入了拥有超过 18000 个"词素"（morphemes，最小的构词单位）的数据库。所以从声音角度我们也能量化：可靠感是什么声音？生命力是什么声音？拿 Sonos 来说，我们想要偏"吵"一点的感觉，所以 S 是个吵的字母，像 Z、甚至 V 也是。于是你开始排定要用哪些字母的优先级。这部分工作，我们叫"工程层"，会往上汇入创意团队。所以在某个时间点上，它是多种东西的融合。（00:26:27）好，那所有这些最后怎么了？通常在开始 3 到 4 周后，我们可能攒出两三千个想法。我说"想法"，是因为它们不都是答案，不都可行，可能只是萌芽、是概念。然后我们筛。我们现在面临、客户也面临的一大挑战，是要做商标查重，不能和市场上已有的冲突——现在这个名字清理的难度，几乎快到临界点了。所以我们有法务助理、有商标律师，会去分析这些名字，把它缩到一个小得多的集合。然后我们和语言学家做语言学工作，最终得到一批要拿给客户的名字。（00:27:22）大多数项目我们会做两轮。有时候受时间和预算限制只做一轮。但我们真的很想做两轮，部分原因是人天生爱比较。你找房子，不会看第一套就说"行，签了吧"，你会看，然后才意识到"我们不需要泳池，但我们需要景"。名字也一样。所以我们会从客户那里拿反馈。有时这是个共创过程：客户想出一个词或方案，我们替他们跑一遍筛选机制。这就是整个流程。最后一个阶段是落地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually pause at that because I would, so much, I want to talk about with the second step, but we'll get to the step three. They're just blowing my mind, all the things you guys do here. This is incredible. There's so many things here that are so unlike what I expected. (00:28:23): First of all, the creative folks that are actually coming up with these names, what's the background of these people? Who are these people?
turns.zh: 咱们先在这儿停一下，因为关于第二步我有太多想聊的，但第三步我们待会儿再说。你们做的这些事，真的让我大开眼界，太了不起了。有太多地方和我预想的完全不一样。（00:28:23）首先，那些真正想出这些名字的创意人员，他们的背景是什么？都是些什么人？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: So, the fundamental quality is they're going to be curious and they're going to be hardworking. This is... And hopefully... And this is hard to screen for, but lower egos. This is unlike the advertising business which I came from, so I've six years at a large agency. Where a creative person or a copywriter can think about something and come in with 3 or 4 alternatives in terms of a headline or body copy. And that might be refined a little bit and maybe sent back to the drawing boards altogether, but it's a relatively simple process. And no disrespect intended there. (00:29:19): Here, I can't just sit down and say, "Okay, we're naming a new car here. And so, I'm going to generate 100 names and you generate 100 names, and something will fall out." Those names will not... There's not enough in that list to clear through our screens. Of legal screens, our linguistic screens. And remember, we start with a creative framework and a criteria that the names need to meet. So, we're looking for people who can churn out a lot of work. And when that's rejected, they just keep going. So, we look for tenacious people. Now, we have... And we'll probably get to this later, but we have software here that helps people generate names. Not really... Maybe five years down the road, it'll actually spit out solutions, but now it's helping us to generate ideas and directions and what I... Sound symbolism, ideas, word unit, prefixes, suffixes, things like that. So, it's relatively easy for anyone that works here to develop a list of 2 or 300 names over a 3 or 4-day period. (00:30:41): Where do we find these people? More who are writers from newspaper reporters because they have to work fast. Their stories get rejected. People who might have written a novel. We have hired people from agencies over the years. They work a little less effectively than others who have a speechwriter from... I wrote speeches in Washington. Those people have to work hard, crank out a lot of material, get rejected. Candidate says, "I don't like this, start over." Those are more resilient people. That's where they come from. It's not easy to find these people. It really isn't.
turns.zh: 最根本的素质是：好奇，而且肯下苦功。还有——这点很难筛——就是 ego 要低。这和我之前待的广告业不一样，我在一家大广告公司干过六年。在那儿，一个创意人或文案想个东西，带来三四个标题或正文的备选，稍微打磨一下，或者整体打回重做，是个相对简单的过程。我没有任何不敬的意思。（00:29:19）但在我们这儿，我不能一坐下来就说："好，我们在给一辆新车取名，我来生成 100 个、你生成 100 个，总会有个能用的。"那些名字根本过不了我们的筛子——法律的筛子、语言学的筛子。别忘了，我们是从创意框架和一套名字必须满足的标准起步的。所以我们要找能大量产出的人，而且被否了还能接着干。我们要找有韧劲的人。我们现在……这个可能待会儿再细说，但我们有一套软件帮人生成名字。也不完全是……也许五年后它能直接吐出答案，但现在它帮我们产出想法、方向，还有我说的语音象征、词素、前缀后缀那些。所以在这里工作的人，三四天内攒出两三百个名字的清单，相对容易。（00:30:41）我们从哪儿找这些人？更多是报社记者出身的写作者，因为他们必须写得快、稿子常被毙。还有写过小说的人。这些年我们也从广告公司招过人，但他们干得不如另一类人效率高——比如给……我在华盛顿写过演讲稿。那种人必须拼命干、大量产出、被拒绝。候选人说"我不喜欢，重来"，他们顶得住。这种人更有韧性。他们就是从这些地方来的。找到这种人不容易，真的不容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me just throw out here. I'm going to ask you after we go through this process, what people that don't have the resources and time to do this, what they should do to come up with a good name. I'm just going to let people know as they're listening because-
turns.zh: 我先把一句话撂这儿。等咱们走完这套流程，我会问你：那些没资源、没时间做这套的人，该怎么想出一个好名字。我想趁大家还在听的时候先透个底，因为——

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... I imagine many people are wondering, but let's not go there yet.
turns.zh: ……我猜很多人正琢磨这事儿，不过咱们先不急。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long does this process usually take? What's the ideal length the company should expect when they want to come up with an amazing name?
turns.zh: 这套流程一般要多久？一家公司想取个绝妙名字，理想上要预留多长时间？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: For us, the ideal link is pretty short. It's eight weeks. For larger corporate projects where you have boards and a little more politicking to do, and a few more presentations, it's a three-month churn. And sometimes by the time they approve things and clear, it's a four-months process.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，理想周期其实挺短的，八周。如果是更大的企业项目，有董事会、要搞点政治博弈、要多做几场提案，那就是三个月的拉锯。有时候等他们批完、查完重，整件事要拖到四个月。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So eight weeks mostly if you're a big company with a lot of red tape. You have to work through then longer. (00:32:11): Okay, this point you made about three different teams with different almost context is so interesting. So say, let's use Windsurf as an example, which is an amazing name, killing it, that you guys helped come up with. So is the idea there, okay, here's we're naming this AI IDE. One of the team has told, "No, you're building a bicycle. Here's all the same brief, but it's a bicycle. And then another team, you're building a..." I don't know, lap. I don't know, something non-technical essentially, right?
turns.zh: 好，明白了。所以八周多半是那种流程很多的大公司的情况，你得多花时间走完那些流程。（00:32:11）你刚才说的三个不同团队、拿到的几乎是不同背景这点，太有意思了。就拿 Windsurf 举例吧——这是个超棒的名字，现在火得不行，是你们帮忙想出来的。所以思路是这样的：好，我们要给这个 AI IDE 取名。其中一个队被告知"不，你们在做一辆自行车"，简报内容都一样，但它是辆自行车。然后另一个队，你们在做……我也不知道，某种……总之是个本质上非技术的东西，对吧？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like, a cup. Say more about that because that is amazing because. And you're finding that most of the best names come from the groups that aren't... Let's name an amazing AI IDE.
turns.zh: 比如一个杯子。再多说说，因为这真的太妙了。而且你们发现，大多数最好的名字，恰恰出自那些不是……"我们来给一个超棒 AI IDE 取名"的组。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: This is a good example. So in technology, there are some things that if someone hands you a new phone and you look at it and it's tangible and it's got a shape and color, things like that, easier to name. But the name of Windsurf, before it was Windsurf, was Codium. So, it's all about a type of code or a process for coding. That's intangible. And even though we do an awful lot of technology work, it is still hard for us to really get ahold of what that is. So our rule here is if there's something that is intangible like that, we have to make it tangible. And sometimes we do that not by giving a team, sometimes it's an individual, the assignment to create ideas for the brand itself, but to just dive into a particular context. (00:33:49): And in this case with Windsurf, this is about flow about giving people that are coding something much more of a flow process, a smoother process, a more dynamic process. So in that case, One team was just given the task of we want to look at a list of all the things that can communicate either in a real word like flow or metaphorically or in a sport about that kind of dynamics. That kind of movement. And there was Windsurf sitting on a list. I mean, sometimes, this is really just that simple. Of course, you have to have the right framework and you have to give the right directions to someone. And Windsurf, for us and particularly for me, it checks all the boxes. It's a wonderful image, it's an experience. Literally, a physical experience. It's a compound, right? Two words put together. We know from the research we've invested in that compounds like Powerbook or Facebook are multipliers of associations because there's wind and there's circles around that, and then there's surf images around that. So 1 + 1 = 3, right? (00:35:16): It's interesting that when we present compounds to clients, we often get the comment, "Well, it's a little bit long and it's a compound. I'd rather have a shorter single word." And then that's why we actually did research on just how effective our compounds so we could pass that information along. We passed that along to the team at that time. Codium, by the way, could not have been a more intelligent, nicer, more respectful team that we've worked with. I'm so glad for their success. But we explained to them about the multiplier effect of compounds. We showed them imagery that they could use. I mean, it's simple to execute on something like that. And so, that's how that came about. I'll stop there and see if you need more information or not.
turns.zh: 这是个好例子。在技术里，有些东西——比如有人递给你一部新手机，你看得到、摸得着，有形状有颜色——比较好取名。但 Windsurf 在叫 Windsurf 之前，叫 Codium，讲的是某种代码类型或编码流程，是抽象的、摸不着的。虽然我们做了大量的技术类项目，但要真正抓住那种东西还是很难。所以我们的规矩是：遇到这种抽象的东西，就得把它变具体。有时候我们不是让一个团队——有时甚至是一个人——去为品牌本身想点子，而是让他们直接扎进某个具体情境里。（00:33:49）拿 Windsurf 来说，它关乎"flow"（心流/流畅），是想让写代码的人获得更顺畅、更顺滑、更有动感的过程。所以当时我们给一个队布置的任务就是：列一张清单，找出所有能传达这种动态的东西——要么用像 flow 这种实在的词，要么用比喻，要么用一项运动。那种流动感、那种运动。然后 Windsurf 就躺在清单上。有时候真的就这么简单。当然，前提是你得有对的框架，得给对人方向。而 Windsurf，对我们、尤其对我个人来说，方方面面都对了。它是个很棒的画面，是个体验，说白了是一种身体上的体验。它是个复合词，对吧？两个词拼在一起。我们从投入的研究里知道，像 Powerbook、Facebook 这种复合词，能让联想成倍放大——有风，风周围有回旋，还有冲浪的画面。所以 1+1=3，对吧？（00:35:16）有意思的是，我们把复合词拿给客户时，经常听到这样的反馈："嗯，有点长，还是复合词，我更想要个短一点的单词。"所以后来我们专门做了研究，看复合词到底多有效，好把这些信息传出去。当时我们就把研究结论给了那个团队。顺便说，Codium 团队是我们合作过的最聪明、最友善、最尊重人的团队，没有之一。我真心为他们现在的成功高兴。但我们给他们解释了复合词的放大效应，也给他们看了可以用的视觉素材。这种事执行起来其实很简单。它就是这么来的。我先讲到这儿，看你还想不想了解更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me actually follow this through real quick. It's going to be kind of a tangent. You guys have been working with AI companies more and more recently, which is so interesting. What's different about naming AI products from traditional products, not AI, I guess?
turns.zh: 我顺着这个快速追问一下，可能有点跑题。你们最近和 AI 公司合作得越来越多，这特别有意思。给 AI 产品取名，和给传统（非 AI）产品取名，到底有什么不同？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: First off, we are working mostly with engineers, and engineers who haven't delved into the world of creativity and necessarily marketing. And that's their strength. And what we have to do is we have to balance their strength with our strength. So there's a little bit of a challenge there, but I think we deal pretty well with that. Secondly, this is the fastest moving progressing category I have ever experienced. And I have that perspective, right? I went through the early days of the internet and the World Wide Web, and that was moving pretty fast. But the internet compared to this looks like a daycare school or something like that. We're challenged by just keeping up with developments. Third thing, and this is the creative challenge here, is that engineers come to us wanting more sophisticated names where they are likely to end up with another Codium or an Anduril or an Anthropic. (00:37:42): And when we saw this trend of that AI is going to take off, and it was an intuitive feeling on my part. I could have been wrong. I said, "Let's find out what's going on here." So both, not only who's developing the products, but how do people think about AI? And we did a series of research. I probably invested $20,000 or so. And we interviewed consumers in Europe, South Korea, just picked out one country in Asia, and in America, and developers in those three. And they really have different views. Developers are all totally positive on it. They see the future, they see a big future, not too concerned, some are, but most aren't. Consumers are skeptical, worried about it, worried about their jobs, see the hope in it, those types of things, but haven't got the handle on it. (00:38:41): So Codium is an example where we said, "We think what you're doing needs to be much more tangible, and something that people can grab onto, and much more natural as opposed to a Codium." And they listened to us. Very simple as that. And in this case, we were right. And by the way also, I have to say, there's some luck to this. Windsurf happened to be available and they sought right away, not exactly right away but it took about a week going back and forth to select it. So, let me stop there and see if that answers your question.
turns.zh: 首先，我们合作的主要是工程师，而且是不一定深入过创意或营销世界的工程师。但这恰恰是他们强的地方。我们要做的，是把他们的优势和我们的优势平衡起来。所以这里有点挑战，但我觉得我们处理得挺好。第二，这是我经历过变化最快的一个品类。我是有这个参照的，对吧？我经历过互联网和万维网早期，那已经够快了。但互联网跟这个比，简直像个托儿所。光是跟上发展节奏，我们就够呛。第三，这是个创意上的挑战：工程师来找我们时，往往想要更"高深"的名字，结果很容易落到又一个 Codium、Anduril 或 Anthropic 那种调性。（00:37:42）当初我们看到 AI 要起飞这个趋势，那是我个人的直觉，也可能错。我说："咱们搞清楚这到底是怎么回事。"所以不仅要看谁在做产品，还要看人们怎么看待 AI。我们做了一系列调研，大概投了 2 万美元。我们采访了欧洲、韩国（就亚洲挑了一个国家）、还有美国的消费者，以及这三个地方的开发者。他们的看法真的很不一样。开发者全都是完全正面的，他们看到未来、看到大未来，不太担心——有些人担心，但大多数不。消费者则持怀疑态度，担心它、担心自己的工作，但也看得到希望，总之还没完全搞明白。（00:38:41）所以 Codium 就是个例子：我们跟他们说"我们认为你们做的事需要更具体、更让人抓得住、更自然，而不是 Codium 这种"。他们听了我们的。就这么简单。而这次我们是对的。另外我必须说，这里面也有运气成分。Windsurf 恰好能注册，他们很快——也不算特别快，来回挑了大概一周——就定下了它。我先讲到这儿，看这有没有回答你的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And it feels like most AI companies end up having a different name for their product than their company. I've noticed this funny trend cursor was any sphere bold with stack is StackBlitz, Windsurf is Codium. Basically, everyone. (00:39:37): When does it make sense to change your name? Windsurf just officially changed their entire company name to Windsurf from Codium. It was just a product. So, let me just ask you that. When does it make sense? It feels like a huge deal and a very challenging thing to do.
turns.zh: 完全对。而且我感觉大多数 AI 公司产品和公司最终用的是不同的名字。我注意到一个挺好笑的趋势：Cursor 背后的公司是 Anysphere，StackBlitz 背后是另一家，Windsurf 背后是 Codium。基本上家家如此。（00:39:37）那什么时候才值得改名字？Windsurf 刚刚把整个公司名从 Codium 正式改成了 Windsurf——之前那只是个产品名。所以我就想问你：什么时候改名字才划算？这感觉是件大事，而且做起来非常有挑战。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: It is challenging. And the larger you are and the more customer base you have, it becomes a significant project. So the first thing is you have to make an argument that it's worth the change. That we're going to be better off by changing our name. So, there's a couple situations where you want to change your name. First one is let's focus first on startups. Startups get going early, they get into Y Combinator or something like that, they're raising money. And they just need a name. And although they know what they're doing, and that may change by 10 or 15 degrees, it's almost like, "We just got to have a name." And that is the absolute expression I hear from when a startup calls and says, "We want to change your name. We started off a year and a half ago. We just needed a name for the documents, and so we chose X." And it's not a very good name. So, that's example number one. (00:40:53): Number two is the company actually has pivoted. And so, the name that they have no longer really reflects who they are or who they're becoming, and which makes that name ineffective. And the third is that a company has merged and it is time now to create a new start and reflect to the marketplace that we're... We're new now, maybe bigger, but certainly we have more capabilities and we want you to know about it. And because of that, we're changing our to blank, which reflects those capabilities at some level.
turns.zh: 这很有挑战性。你体量越大、客户基础越广，改名字就越是个大工程。所以第一件事是，你得论证"改名字是值得的"，改了之后我们会更好。想改名字，一般就几种情况。先说初创公司。初创公司起步早，进了 Y Combinator 之类的，在融资。他们就是需要个名字。虽然他们知道自己要做什么，方向可能也就偏个十度十五度，但当时就是"我们得先有个名字"。这是我常从初创公司那儿听到的原话："我们想改名字。一年半前刚起步，只是给文件要个名，就选了 X。"而那并不是个好名字。这是第一种情况。（00:40:53）第二种，是这家公司真的转型了。所以现有的名字已经不能反映他们是谁、在变成谁，于是这个名字就失效了。第三种，是公司合并了，是时候重新出发，向市场表明"我们变了——也许更大了，但肯定能力更强了，想让你知道"。正因如此，我们把名字改成空白，在某种程度上体现那些能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to have Andrew Luo joining us today. Andrew is CEO of OneSchema, one of our longtime podcast sponsors. Welcome, Andrew.
turns.zh: 今天很高兴有 Andrew Luo 加入我们。Andrew 是 OneSchema 的 CEO，也是我们这个播客的老牌赞助商。欢迎你，Andrew。

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请，Lenny。很高兴来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what is new with OneSchema? I know that you work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp and Vanta and Watershed. I heard you guys launched a new data intake product that automates the hours of manual work that teams spent importing, and mapping, and integrating CSV in Excel files.
turns.zh: OneSchema 最近有什么新动静？我知道你们和几家我很喜欢的公司合作，比如 Ramp、Vanta 和 Watershed。我听说你们推出了一款新的数据接入产品，能把团队在导入、映射、整合 CSV 和 Excel 文件上花的好几个小时的手动工作自动化。

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Yes. So, we just launched the 2.0 of OneSchema FileFeeds. We've rebuilt it from the ground up with AI. We saw so many customers coming to us with teams of data engineers that struggled with the manual work required to clean messy spreadsheets. FileFeeds 2.0 allows non-technical teams to automate the process of transforming CSV in Excel files with just a simple prompt. We support all of the trickiest file integrations, SFTP, S3, and even email.
turns.zh: 对。我们刚发布了 OneSchema FileFeeds 2.0。我们用 AI 从零重构了它。我们看到太多客户带着数据工程师团队来找我们，他们被清理乱糟糟表格的手动工作折磨得够呛。FileFeeds 2.0 让非技术团队只需一句简单的提示词，就能把 CSV 和 Excel 文件的转换过程自动化。我们支持所有最棘手的档案集成方式，SFTP、S3，甚至邮件都行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to take this off our roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema.
turns.zh: 我跟你说，如果我的团队得自己搭这种集成，能把这从我们的路线图里拿掉、改用 OneSchema 这种东西，那得有多爽。

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of outages from even just a single bad record in transactions, employee files, purchase orders, you name it. Debugging these issues is often like finding a needle in a haystack. OneSchema stops any bad data from entering your system and automatically validates your files, generating error reports with the exact issues in all bad files.
turns.zh: 绝对，Lenny。我们听过太多恐怖故事了——哪怕只是一笔交易、一份员工档案、一张采购单里有一条坏记录，都能导致系统宕机，不一而足。排查这些问题常常像大海捞针。OneSchema 能拦住任何坏数据进入你的系统，自动校验你的文件，并生成错误报告，指出所有坏文件里的确切问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Andrew, thank you so much for joining me. If you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co, That's oneschema.co. (00:43:12): I want to come back to this linguist piece, which I know is really unique to the way you guys operate, and it's so interesting. So you employed, you've said, over 250 linguists over the course of your business career. This linguist step, the way you described it is they're not coming up with names, they're more kind of like a filter for, "Here's all the names we've come up with. Here's the ones that are good linguistically." Is that right? Or is that team also suggesting names?
turns.zh: 我知道，导入错误数据会给你的客户带来各种麻烦，还会迅速失去他们的信任。Andrew，非常感谢你的参与。想了解更多，去 oneschema.co，就是 oneschema.co。（00:43:12）我想回到"语言学家"这块，我知道这是你们运作方式里特别独特、也特别有意思的一环。你说过，你整个职业生涯雇佣过 250 多位语言学家。你描述的这个语言学家环节，听起来他们不是来想名字的，更像是道筛子——"这是我们想出来的所有名字，这些是语言学上过关的"。是这样吗？还是这个团队也会提名字？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah. Some of the people there, depending on the assignment, will actually help us create names, for sure. And so, we have linguists here. And in the network, we have linguists. And those linguists are contracts to us, not full-time employees. So, there's a little bit of both. But the preponderance of their work in our linguistic network is to evaluate names. Not only just does it mean something negative or positive, but are there cultural implications to it? Political implications? Or even things that a natural disaster that would've happened somewhere that no one here would know about. Even if we had, if. (00:44:21): This was in Italy, and there was a bridge or a flood that killed a lot of people. Someone that speaks Italian very well here, say at Berkeley University, but has lived here for 20 years, wouldn't know about that. And we don't want anything linguistically that would slow our clients down. And so, that's why we've invested in building this network. We have a woman that runs the network for it. So, it's not an insignificant facet of our business that we have to run and manage.
turns.zh: 对。那里的一些人，看具体任务，确实也会帮我们想名字。我们内部有语言学家，网络里也有语言学家。网络里的那些是和我们签约的，不是全职员工。所以两种情况都有一点。但在我们的语言学网络里，他们的工作大头是评估名字。不只是看它意思是好是坏，还要看它有没有文化上的引申？政治上的？甚至某个地方发生过一场自然灾害，这儿没人知道。就算我们……如果……（00:44:21）比如意大利，有一座桥塌了或者一场洪水，死了很多人。一个意大利语说得很好、比如在伯克利大学的人，但在美国住了 20 年，就不会知道这事。而我们不想要任何会在语言学上拖客户后腿的东西。所以这就是为什么我们花力气建了这张网络。我们有位女士专门负责运营它。所以这不是我们业务中一个无足轻重的环节，而是要认真运营和管理的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a name you love that didn't pass the linguistic filter, that ended up being like, "Oh, shit. That's a really bad name in this culture"?
turns.zh: 有没有那种你特别喜欢、却没过语言学筛子的名字，最后变成"糟了，这文化里这名字太烂了"？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: It happens frequently where we will find something that isn't really terrible but it's worrisome to us. It's interesting cultures like Australian or people in Australia, they have a lot of interesting expressions. And so, we do find things that this sounds like it's a certain kind of shrimp and things like that, and we eliminate those things. And then we find things that have sort of sexual connotations, we eliminate those. (00:45:39): I would say it happens every third or fourth project we'll find something that we will eliminate and never show the client.
turns.zh: 经常发生。我们会发现一些不算真的很糟、但让我们心里犯嘀咕的东西。有意思的是，像澳大利亚这种文化，有很多有趣的俚语。所以我们确实会碰到听起来像某种虾、之类的词，然后把它淘汰掉。还有那些带点性暗示的，我们也淘汰。（00:45:39）我可以说，差不多每三四个项目里，就会有一个我们淘汰掉、永远不给客户看的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And something you love and you're like, "Okay, I guess we can show that one"?
turns.zh: 那有没有那种你很喜欢、然后想"行吧，这大概能拿给客户看"的？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: That's true. That happens. It does.
turns.zh: 有的，确实有这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You also said this really interesting thing about how every letter of the alphabet has a vibrance in an experience. Can you give a few examples of that? I know you're not the person doing that work specifically, but just what are some letter feelings?
turns.zh: 你还说过一个特别有意思的点：字母表里每个字母都有一种"鲜活感"和体验。你能举几个例子吗？我知道具体干这活儿的不是你，但随便说说几个字母的感觉？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: The work is from the linguist, but at this point, I'm pretty adept in it. So, let's look at... I'll start with the letter V because it is so illustrative of what this is about. V, from our research that we've done, is the most alive and vibrant sound in the English alphabet. And that's whether you were born in Rome or in Sausalito, California. So if you know that, if you know that as you go around the world, there are going to be some exceptions to it. It's going to have that vibrancy. Look at Corvette. They probably didn't know about V, but it's a perfect name for a car that's fast and has a big engine that roars. Think about Viagra, same idea. And there's been surprises to us. B, the sound of the letter B is one of the most reliable sounds in the English alphabet. That was one of our rationales, by the way, for Blackberry. Because that's another example of a client who thought we were... I mean, the founder actually said, "I thought the people at Lexicon were crazy," when they presented Blackberry. (00:47:29): And we said, "Well, let's stop and look at some of the assets here. First off, black color's technology. Yes, not everybody knows the word berry, but we have those two Bs." We talked about the nature of a compound. And all of a sudden, people at least lean forward to consider it as opposed to rejecting it too fast. So, those are just two examples. I mentioned Z in Azure, that's noisy letter. X is fast and crisp as a sound. And of course, there's semantic value to all of these letters, too. X is about innovation from aircraft to computers. And so, you have to look at the semantics of it and the sound symbol of it.
turns.zh: 这活儿是语言学家做的，但到这个阶段，我也算很熟练了。那我们看……先从字母 V 说起，因为它最能说明这回事。根据我们的研究，V 是英文字母里最"有生命力"、最鲜活的声音。不管你生在罗马，还是加州 Sausalito，都一样。所以你要知道，走到全世界，可能会有少数例外，但它就是有那种鲜活感。看看 Corvette（科尔维特）。他们当年大概不知道 V 这回事，但对一辆又快、引擎又轰鸣的车来说，这是个完美的名字。想想 Viagra（伟哥），也是同样的道理。而且也有让我们意外的。B 这个音，是英文字母里最"可靠"的声音之一。顺便说，这也是我们选 Blackberry 的理由之一。因为这也是个客户以为我们……我是说，创始人当初看到 Blackberry 时，原话是"我以为 Lexicon 那帮人疯了"。（00:47:29）而我们说："好，咱们停下来看看手里的牌。首先，黑色是科技感。没错，不是每个人都认识 berry 这个词，但我们还有那两个 B。"我们讲了复合词的本质。然后人们至少会前倾身体、愿意考虑它，而不是太快否决。所以这只是两个例子。我提过 Azure 里的 Z，那是个吵的字母。X 的声音又快又脆。当然，这些字母也都有语义价值。X 代表着从飞机到计算机的创新。所以你得同时看它的语义和声音象征。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so fascinating. I could listen to this stuff all day. Just thinking about Vercel with the V, that very aligns with what they're trying to do. Just very strong, opinionated way of working. And Guillermo, he feels like a V person.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这东西我能听一整天。光想 Vercel 里的那个 V，就特别契合他们想做的事——非常强、非常有主见的工作方式。而且 Guillermo，他就是个 V 型人格。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: He is. And there's an example of a group that had a lot of confidence, and what their product is is very innovative. And so, we had permission there to create something new because Vercel is a coin solution., right? But notice that we put some very simple, easy to process things together there. Or ver, in this case. So we have in vino veritas, truth in wine, things like that. You have verde, green. So, very familiar. And then their cel, like accelerate, something which is really what they do. They accelerate a client's performance. So, that was a relatively easy name for us to present and we were excited about for them to grasp. (00:49:26): By the way, that's known as processing fluency, which is when you think about how the brain processes information. We're told by a number of cognitive science that our brains are a little bit on the lazy side. We don't like complex things. And so, we really strive to make all of our solutions relatively easy for the brain to process. So it wants, it leans in towards them as opposed to, "I'm too busy. I'm walking past that." Names that are complicated, it's a liability. And we really avoid that. But Vercel, perfect fluency.
turns.zh: 他是。这也是个例子：一个很有自信的团队，他们的产品非常创新。所以在 Vercel 上，我们有空间去创造新东西，因为它是一个"造词"方案，对吧？但你注意，我们在里面放了一些非常简单、好处理的元素。比如 ver。所以我们有 in vino veritas（酒中真言）、verde（绿色）这种，大家都很熟。然后是 cel，像 accelerate（加速）——而这正是他们干的事，他们让客户的性能加速。所以对我们来，这是个相对好提的名字，我们也兴奋地盼着他们能接住。（00:49:26）顺便说，这叫"加工流畅度"（processing fluency），讲的是大脑怎么处理信息。好几位认知科学家告诉我们，大脑有点"懒"，不喜欢复杂的东西。所以我们极力让我们所有的方案都相对好让大脑处理。这样大脑会主动"凑过来"，而不是"我太忙了，走过路过就算了"。复杂的名字是负资产，我们真的很回避。但 Vercel，流畅度满分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's go back, actually, to the three steps. So we covered two, and it took us on a long tangent to dive into a lot of the stuff you shared with the second step, which you call invent. So, it's essentially the three steps are... Was it create? What would you call it? The step?
turns.zh: 好，咱们其实回到那三个步骤。我们已经聊了两个，而且为了深挖第二步（你叫"发明"）里你分享的很多内容，我们扯了很远。所以本质上这三步是……是"创造"吗？你怎么叫这步？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah, it's identify. Invent.
turns.zh: 对，是识别（identify）、发明（invent）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Identify.
turns.zh: 识别。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: And I use the word invent with intention because it's more than creative. And then the final thing is implement. Now for us, we're not a design firm. We're really focused on brand names and the nomenclature that supports the name. But for us, implement is helping the client team, if they choose, for us to help them with the presentations as it goes up the chain. To help them write a longer rationale for why these names, if they're presenting three names to the president of their company or the CMO, why these names make a lot of sense, and to help them develop what we call prototypes. So we'll put the name on a baseball cap, on a T-shirt. We'll put the name in a mock-up ad in the Wall Street Journal. Something's very positive. Because of Procter & Gamble's new blank product. P&G shares, they gain 10% this year. So that executives can see that the lift that that name can have. That's our implementation phase for them. (00:51:44): And we also do consumer research or customer research at that stage, and we do that probably about 50% of the time on our projects where we're going out and we're really talking to their customers, and putting the names in a series of drills. Drills that make them not the marketing person for the day, but we're really making these customers feel that this is a new brand. And then, we're asking about expectations. We're seeing how these names fire their imagination. And that's the most important thing in research, not is the name popular, are they comfortable with it, does it fit to concept. If you're asking people is this fit to concept, you are inevitably always going to get a descriptive name.
turns.zh: 我用"发明"这个词是刻意的，因为它不只是创意。最后一步是落地（implement）。对我们来说，我们不是设计公司，我们真正聚焦的是品牌名，以及支撑这个名字的命名体系。但"落地"对我们来说，是——如果客户愿意——帮他们的团队把方案一层层往上汇报时做准备。帮他们写一份更充分的论证，说明为什么是这几个名字：如果他们要向公司总裁或 CMO 提三个名字，为什么这几个名字很有道理，并且帮他们做出我们所谓的"原型"。比如我们会把名字印在棒球帽上、T 恤上，或者放进《华尔街日报》的一则模拟广告里，呈现非常正面的样子："因为宝洁这款全新的空白产品，宝洁股价今年涨了 10%。"这样高管就能看到这个名字能带来的提升。这就是我们为他们的落地阶段。（00:51:44）在那个阶段我们也会做消费者或客户调研，大概一半的项目会这么做——我们走出去，真去和他们客户聊，把名字放进一系列"演练"里。这些演练会让受访者那一刻不是"今天的市场人员"，而是真的让他们感觉这是一个新品牌。然后我们去问期望，看这些名字怎么点燃他们的想象力。而这是调研里最重要的事——不是问"这个名字流不流行""你舒不舒服""它契不契合概念"。如果你问人"它契不契合概念"，你注定只会得到一个描述性的名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You make such a good point about how you need to arm the people working with you with ammo to win over other folks internally. Because if the person working with you is on board and the name is bold and not an obvious winner, I could see it being important to be like, "Here's what you should all show them to help them see the story, and the mock-ups, and all of that."
turns.zh: 你说得太对了：你得给和你合作的人"弹药"，好让他们去内部说服其他人。因为如果和你对接的人自己认同了，而名字又很大胆、不是那种一眼看出的赢家，我就觉得这很重要——"这是你们该拿去给他们看的，帮他们看见那个故事、那些原型图，等等"。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes. And what's really important is to help their management see this in the context of the marketplace and their customers. This is a very human thing, but people want their boss to be happy. They want to be okay with their boss. And so they're thinking about, "I don't know if my boss would like this." He's more conservative or she's more conservative. We try in a very diplomatic way to say, "This has nothing, really, in the end to do with your boss. It has to do with the marketplace." (00:53:27): Well, that's easy for me to say because I'm not working at a P&G or an Intel, but we really try to give that advice for it because it is about being successful in the marketplace. And so first of all, we try to separate the clients that we work with. We really want to work with clients that play to win, that want to win, not just want to not lose in a marketplace. And so, we try to encourage our direct clients to lead the process to really say, if a manager or a CMO or a president says, "Look, we're the team that's going to execute on this and we believe in this. We can make this work," they usually rally around it. They usually do. But if you're just taking names up to a manager and saying, "What do you think?" There's a different outcome offered. (00:54:28): So, we like to be in that implementation phase because we have so much experience. And usually, credibility with people.
turns.zh: 对。真正重要的是，帮他们的管理层在市场和大客户的语境里看这件事。这是很人性的事——人总想让老板高兴，想和老板处好。所以他们会想"我不知道我老板喜不喜欢这个"，老板更保守些。我们会用很委婉的方式说："说到底，这跟你老板没啥关系，它跟市场有关。"（00:53:27）嗯，这话我说着容易，毕竟我不在宝洁或英特尔上班，但我们真的很想给这种建议，因为这关乎在市场上成不成。所以首先，我们会筛选合作客户。我们真心想和"志在必得"、想赢的客户合作，而不只是想"别输"的客户。所以我们会鼓励直接对接的客户去主导这个过程，真正说出"看，我们就是来执行这个的团队，我们信这个，我们能把它做成"——这种话一出，大家通常会团结起来。通常会的。但如果你只是把名字递给经理问"你觉得呢？"，结果就完全不一样了。（00:54:28）所以我们喜欢待在落地这个阶段，因为我们经验太丰富了，通常也能让人信服。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said that you come up with 3 to 4,000 names. That's the top of the funnel?
turns.zh: 你说过你们会想出三四千个名字。那是漏斗的顶端？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah. And just to clarify that, it's ideas, directions. It's not-
turns.zh: 对。澄清一下，那是想法、方向，不是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Complete ready-to-ship names.
turns.zh: 不是那种可以直接上线的成品名字。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah, not ready-to-ship names at all.
turns.zh: 对，完全不是可以直接上线的名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: This is a very inefficient process and a little chaotic. So in that list of 3,000 names is probably 250 potential diamonds that have to be fractured and examined.
turns.zh: 这是个效率很低、还有点乱的过程。所以在那 3000 个名字的清单里，大概有 250 颗"潜在的钻石"，得切开、得检验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really want to see just a documentary of this process at some point. This is the closer we're going to get for now, but this is so interesting. (00:55:17): I want to ask about how you would approach this if you're just a startup that doesn't have the time or resource to do this. But before I do that, is there anything else around the process that you guys go through with clients that you think is important to share or they think might surprise people?
turns.zh: 我真的好想哪天看一部讲这个流程的纪录片。这大概是我们目前能最接近它的方式了，但真的太有意思了。（00:55:17）我想问的是，如果你只是个没时间、没资源做这套的初创公司，你会怎么走。不过在那之前，关于你们和客户走的这套流程，还有什么你觉得重要、或者可能让人意外的，想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: I think we've covered it. I do.
turns.zh: 我觉得都聊到了。确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Awesome. Okay, so most people listening to this, there's a lot of founders, a lot of PMs on product teams. They're working on a new feature, they're about to launch a product, they got accepted into YC and they're about to launch a product. Then they have, I don't know, let's say they have a couple of weeks. We've got to come up with a name. What should they do?
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。好，听这期的大多数人，很多是创始人、很多是产品团队的产品经理。他们在做一个新功能，即将发布一个产品，进了 YC，马上要上线。然后他们……我就说他们有两三周时间，必须想出个名字。他们该怎么办？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: So the first thing I do is to say, okay, let's forget about developing the name for right now. And I will have them, and I think this is a good exercise for anybody. We do it here internally when we think about our business. So I say, just... Because most of this now, because of COVID, is on video. And I will say, "Just draw a shape of a diamond on a piece of paper in front of you." And I said, "On the top of that diamond, put the word win. How do you define winning is really it?" I said, "Now on that other next corner of the diamond, what do you have to win? Write that down. On the bottom, what do you need to win? And then on that final angle on the left-hand side, what do you have to say to win?" Then I said, "Now, let's go all the way to that final thing of what do you have to say to win." (00:56:49): And that's where you just get people thinking about, "Well, what we really have here is... And we're better than this." And then I'll just say, "Okay. Now, what you want to take that this really should be about experience and behavior. How do you want to behave in the marketplace? How do you want the marketplace to behave towards you? And what kind of experience are you creating?" And then they'll start talking a little bit. I'll say, "Now, you just need to probe on that. You need to keep going. You need to look at metaphors because this is about experience." And I'll just give them some of our examples that we've talked about, "Blackberry, it says to the marketplace, they're not like the other guys." Think of something like Google versus Infoseek, right? Google is an experience. Google says, "I don't know what these guys are going to do, but it's not this practical mundane Infoseek." And that's what attracts people. (00:57:54): And so I'll do a little coaching like that, and then that usually kind of sets them free. And they're now thinking about it not as a word, which has maybe limited value, but as creating an experience which has the potential for unlimited value.
turns.zh: 所以我做的第一件事是：好，现在先别管去想那个名字。我会让他们做这个——我觉得对任何人都很受用，我们内部思考自己业务时也会做。我会说……因为现在多半是疫情后线上视频，我会说："就在你面前那张纸上，画一个菱形。"我说："在菱形顶端，写上 win（赢）。你怎么定义'赢'才是关键？"我说："然后在菱形的下一个角，写'你必须拿什么去赢'。底部写'你需要什么才能赢'。左边最后一个角，写'你要说出什么才能赢'。"然后我说："好，我们一路走到最后这个——你要说出什么才能赢。"（00:56:49）这一步就是让人开始想："嗯，我们真正拥有的是……而且我们比这更好。"然后我会说："好。现在你要意识到，这其实该关乎体验和行为。你想在市场上怎么表现？你想市场对你怎么表现？你在创造一种什么体验？"然后他们会开始聊一点。我会说："现在你要顺着这个深挖，继续往下，去看比喻，因为这关乎体验。"我会给他们举我们聊过的例子："Blackberry 对市场说的是，他们和别的家伙不一样。"想想 Google 对 Infoseek，对吧？Google 是一种体验。Google 说的是"我不知道这帮人要做啥，但肯定不是那种务实又平庸的 Infoseek"。而这才吸引人。（00:57:54）所以我会做点这样的引导，通常这就把他们解放出来了。他们现在想的不再是一个"词"——那价值有限——而是在创造一种"体验"，而体验有无限的价值潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, let me try to reflect this back for folks. So the advice is draw triangle. So, you're coming up with a name. Draw triangle. At the top, win. At the bottom-left, was it how do you win?
turns.zh: 好。我来帮大家复述一下。所以建议是画个三角形。你要取名字，就画个三角形。顶端写 win。左下角，是"你怎么赢"吗？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah. So, the diamond is two triangles.
turns.zh: 对。菱形其实就是两个三角形拼的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, diamond. Okay, I see. I have triangle in my mind.
turns.zh: 哦，菱形。好，我懂了。我脑子里一直是三角形。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: I got you.
turns.zh: 我懂你意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. Diamond. Great.
turns.zh: 好，明白了。菱形。好。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: And so on that next angle there on the right side is, what do you have to win already? Right? Because they wouldn't be either in a Y Combinator or getting some seed money if they didn't have something to win. And often, people, startups don't appreciate how much they actually do have to win because they're so busy and so stressed on what they're doing. And then, what do they need to win? And then finally, what do you need to say? And then back up to defining what is winning to us? Which, by the way, we start with that question usually on an assignment that we've been awarded. And if we're in a room with five people, all five people have a different definition of what... Their definition of that company winning. And that's good to sort that out because we can move down different avenues from a creative standpoint.
turns.zh: 所以在右边下一个角，是"你已经拥有什么可以去赢"？对吧？因为如果他们没点能赢的东西，根本进不了 YC、拿不到种子轮。而初创公司常常意识不到自己其实已经拥有多少"能赢的牌"，因为他们太忙、太焦虑于手头的事。然后是"他们需要什么才能赢"？最后，"你需要说出什么"？然后回到最开始——"对我们来说，赢到底意味着什么"？顺便说，拿到项目后，我们通常会从这个问题开始。如果我们和五个人在一间屋里，这五个人对"公司赢"的定义个个不同。把这理清是好事，因为从创意角度，我们能顺着不同的路径往下走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's just make sure people have these phrases because this is awesome. And I imagine many people are going to be taking notes and like, "Cool. I'm going to do this." I hope so say the four points of the diamond again just so folks can write it all down.
turns.zh: 咱们一定要把这几个词给大家记牢，因为这太棒了。我猜很多人在做笔记，想着"酷，我要照做"。我希望你再把菱形的四个点说一遍，好让大家全记下来。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: At the top of the diamond is just the word win, and underneath that is how do we define winning for us as a company. And that can start off being simple, like we want to be the dominant player here. But you really have to work at that. What does that really mean, right? The second on that right-hand tip there of the diamond is what do we have to win? What are we doing now that makes us a winner? Then we go down to the bottom of the diamond, and it's what do we need to win? There could be technical things there. People talk about talent and resources. Often there, they'll say, "We need a good name." We always correct that. It's not the good name, it's the right name. (01:00:28): And then finally is what do we need to say? And that's where I say, that's where you want to spend some time in really thinking about all the things you need to say, that you can say or you would even like to say, which maybe right now you can't say. But you want to a name that actually is going to have the flexibility as to when you can say that, it still works. And that gets them into behavior and experience. And that usually launches a really a good discussion with founders internally.
turns.zh: 菱形最顶端就是 win 这个词，下面跟着的是：作为一家公司，我们怎么定义"赢"。一开始可以很简单，比如"我们想在这个领域当老大"。但你真的得往深里抠。那到底意味着什么，对吧？菱形右边那个角，是"我们必须拿什么去赢"？我们现在做的什么让我们成了赢家？然后到菱形底部，是"我们需要什么才能赢"？那里可能是些技术性的东西。人们会聊人才、资源。常常他们会说"我们需要一个好名字"。我们总是纠正：不是好名字，是对的名字。（01:00:28）最后是"我们需要说什么"？我说，这一步你才该花时间，认真想想你所有需要说的、能说的、甚至想说但现在还说不出口的话。而你想要的是一个真有灵活性的名字——等到你能说那些话时，它依然成立。这就把他们引向了"行为"和"体验"。而这通常会引发创始团队内部一场非常棒的探讨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say you have to win though, what you're thinking about there is what is it that you have that will help you win? And then what is it you need to have this win?
turns.zh: 不过你说到"必须拿什么去赢"的时候，你想的是：你手里有什么能帮你赢？以及，你需要什么才能拿下这场胜利？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes, that's right. And all companies are in that same situation. They have a bunch of stuff, but they need... A P&G might say, "We need a good distributor." (01:01:19): "Okay. All right, we'll put that on the list." (01:01:24): And then you might say, "Well, we need in..." When it gets to what do we have to say, we have to say the right things so that a distributor is interested in us. And then you go down an avenue there. Well, what is that? And if you work at it, this is not a one-hour exercise, it may be an exercise repeated over the next 4 or 5 days.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。所有公司都处在同样的处境。他们有一堆东西，但他们还需要……宝洁可能会说"我们需要一个好经销商"。（01:01:19）"好，行，我们把它列上。"（01:01:24）然后你可能会说"嗯，我们需要在……"等到了"我们需要说什么"这一步，我们就得说出对的东西，好让经销商对我们感兴趣。然后你就顺着这条路往下走。那具体是什么呢？而且如果你认真做，这不是一小时的练习，可能是接下来四五天里反复做的练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, you have this diamond. And then the idea is just sit and put names down in a Google Doc, let's say.
turns.zh: 好。所以你有这个菱形。然后思路就是坐下来，把名字写进一个 Google 文档之类的，对吧？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah. And then you start. But there is this... And maybe, it's naivete. I guess, that's probably the best word for this is that, because I do hear this all of the time. "Hey, we've worked at this, we got a list of 200 names, but we don't think there's something there." (01:02:19): And I'll say, "Well, 200 names is not enough. Get to 1,000, 1,500 names and directions. Don't evaluate them. Just generate names, and directions, and ideas, and then have a meeting. And don't evaluate but speculate." What could we do with this name? What's the potential here? There's a lot of overevaluation in our industry. It makes sense. We survive as humans because we figure out what's wrong with this picture. If I want to cross the street, is it safe to cross the street? What's going on? Those kinds of things. You have to counter that. You have to say, "Let's just suspend judgment for a while. And let's do an exercise here where we take these 10 names that we think might work and what are we going to do with it." Because it's how you execute. (01:03:21): Going back to windsurf, as we showed them pictures of people windsurfing and waves and things, if they said, "Ah, that just doesn't work for us at all. I'm very uncomfortable with." Well, then it's not their name. But they leaned into it, "Okay, I can see this. It's easy for us to execute. It's dynamic, it's different." So, that's why we build these prototypes for people. And that's what... I think the best advice I can give to whether it's a startup or someone starting a new cookie company, is it's not just a list of 200 names. It's 10 or 15 lists of 200 names. And it's thinking about what do we have to say here? What behavior? How do we want people to feel in the marketplace about us? I imagine with Google, people felt relief that it wasn't a descriptive name. That there was something new out there in the marketplace.
turns.zh: 对。然后你们就开始。但这里有个……也许叫"天真"吧，我想这词最贴切，因为我一直听到这种话："嘿，我们努力弄了，列了 200 个名字，但觉得这里头没有合适的。"（01:02:19）我会说："嗯，200 个根本不够。冲到 1000、1500 个名字和方向去。别去评判它们。只管生成名字、方向、想法，然后开个会。别评判，去推演。"我们拿这个名字能干什么？它这里有什么潜力？我们这个行业有太多"过度评判"了。这也能理解——人类能活下来，靠的就是找出"这幅图里哪里不对"。我要过马路，安不安全？发生了什么？这类本能。你得住它对抗。你得说："咱们先把判断挂起来一阵子。咱们做个练习：拿这 10 个我们觉得可能行的名字，我们要拿它们做什么？"因为这取决于你怎么执行。（01:03:21）回到 Windsurf，当我们给他们看人们冲浪、海浪那些图，如果他们说"啊，这根本不行，我太不舒服了"，那它就不是他们的名字。但他们迎了上去："好，我能看到这个。我们执行起来很容易，它有动感、不一样。"所以这就是为什么我们为人们做那些原型。我想给的最好的建议——不管你是初创公司，还是开一家新饼干公司——不是列一张 200 个名字的清单，而是列 10 到 15 张、每张 200 个名字的清单。而且要想：我们在这里需要说什么？是什么行为？我们希望市场上的人对我们是什么感觉？我猜当年 Google 出来的时候，人们松了口气——它不是个描述性的名字，市场上终于有了点新东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Infoseek, that's such a descriptive name now that I think about it.
turns.zh: 对。Infoseek，现在想想，真是个太描述性的名字了。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so one more question along these lines. So say, you have a list of let's say 2,000 or 1,000 names. There's this tension between choosing something... Like, as a person that is doing them themselves. Your advice is choose something bold, not something descriptive. You won't know it when you see it. Very hard to do, obviously, when you're doing it by yourself. And you just advise for not losing sight of that piece. Just throwing out things that feel too scary, finding a name that's actually bold as you suggest.
turns.zh: 好，沿这个线再问一个。假设你列了 2000 或 1000 个名字。在选什么之间会有纠结……比如，作为自己一个人干这事儿的人。你的建议是选大胆的，别选描述性的。你看到时不会知道它好。自己一个人做，显然特别难。你就建议大家别丢了这一点——别因为觉得太吓人就扔掉那些东西，去找一个像你说的那样真正大胆的名字。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: First off, we disappear... Human psychology, humans only pay attention to what is new or what is different, I should say. So if you're looking at shoes and they're all black, black, black, black, and then the next pair of shoes is red, that's the first thing you focus on. And so, that usually gives people permission. They'll say, "Okay, I get that." So, look for what is really different between the names that you have on your list, but also what's different from what's out in the marketplace. Then you get a client like Microsoft saying, "Azure is different. There's going to be a lot of cloud stuff and..." There's a relevant point there, Azure is blue. And so, there's a slight logical connection that I think gave them more permission to move forward with it, frankly. But listen, this is not an easy task. I mean, that's why we're in this business, and why I felt we should be specialized because if you start doing design and/or advertising or other things, you can't have the intellectual engine. (01:06:16): You can't acquire the intellectual engine that we have. So I know it's difficult, but it can be done, and you just have to give yourself some time. But stop evaluating. Suspend judgment and speculate. That's my number one advice to people trying to do this on their own. Now, how can you get help? You can talk to your employees, but it's not so much, "What do you think of this name?" It's, "What do you think this name could do for us?" That's a much better question. If you go out and talk to friends who don't work for your company, there's a fun drill that I suggest. I said, "Listen, go out to them and say..." They'll know what you're doing. And say, "You know what? We just have a new competitor and their name is blank. What do you think about that?" (01:07:10): What happens there is you're not asking them to give you an opinion to evaluate a name. You're asking them then what does that name do for you? The information you're getting is that name, they're telling you what that name does for them, how it helps them to imagine, which is a fundamental role of any name. Slight tangent, but I'm going to go to our kind of research. We do mostly quantitative research now, but for years, we did qualitative work. And we still do. But what we found in, we were always looking for the... (01:07:49): I'll set it this way. We were always looking for this answer from consumers. If a consumer said, "I don't really know much about that new product, but I know that they're not like the other guys." That's when we knew we had a good name because they were... Now what happened there? I mean, the technical term that we use is that name will create a predisposition to consider this product because they're not like the other guys, as opposed to, "I already have something like that. I'm busy. I don't need another one of those things. I need something new and different, and hopefully better."
turns.zh: 首先，我们……人类心理学——应该说，人只关注新的、或不同的东西。所以如果你看一堆鞋，全是黑、黑、黑、黑，然后下一双是红的，你第一眼盯上的就是那双红的。所以这通常给了人们"许可"。他们会说"好，我懂了"。所以，去找你清单上的名字之间真正不同的东西，也要找和市面上已有的东西不同的。然后你会遇到像微软这样的客户说"Azure 不一样。外面会有一大堆 cloud 什么的……"这里有个切题的点：Azure 是蓝色。所以有一个轻微的逻辑关联，说实话，那让他们更有理由往前推它。但听着，这任务不轻松。我的意思是，这就是为什么我们干这行，也是为什么我觉得我们得专——因为如果你同时做起设计、广告或其他，你就没法拥有那台"智力引擎"。（01:06:16）你没法买来我们那种智力引擎。所以我知道这很难，但它能做，你只是得给自己一点时间。但别再评判了。把判断挂起来，去推演。这是给想自己干这事的人的头号建议。那怎么获得帮助？你可以和员工聊，但别问"你觉得这名字怎么样"，要问"你觉得这名字能为我们做什么"。那是个好多得的问题。如果你出去和不在这家公司工作的朋友聊，我建议一个好玩的演练。我说："听好，去跟他们说……"他们知道你在干嘛。你说："你知道吗？我们刚多了个竞争对手，他们叫空白。你怎么看？"（01:07:10）这里发生的，是你没在请他们给个意见去评判一个名字。你是在问：那个名字对你做了什么？你得到的信息是——那个名字，他们在告诉你它对他们做了什么、怎么帮他们想象，而那正是一个名字的根本作用。稍微跑个题，但我说说我们的研究。我们现在主要做定量研究，但多年来我们做定性，现在也还在做。我们一直在找……（01:07:49）我这么讲吧。我们一直在消费者那里找这个答案。如果消费者说"我对那个新产品其实不太了解，但我知道他们和别的家伙不一样"，那我们就知道我们有了个好名字，因为他们……那时发生了什么？我用术语说，那个名字会制造一种"倾向"去考虑这个产品，因为他们和别的家伙不一样——而不是"我已经有类似的东西了，我忙，不需要再来一个那种玩意儿，我需要新的、不一样的，最好还更好的"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. That's a good reminder. There's a quote that I found of yours that's exactly along these lines, "If your team is comfortable with the name, chances are you don't have the name yet."
turns.zh: 太棒了。这提醒得好。我找到你说过的一句原话，正好呼应这点："如果你的团队对某个名字感到舒服，那大概率你还没找到真正的名字。"

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes. And by the way, the opposite of that is we look for polarization. We look for tension in a team about arguing about these things, because we think that polarization is a sign of strength in the word. And interesting story, the person who taught me that, honestly, was Andy Grove over the Pentium name, because... And I learned a lot from him. I always say this, I just was very fortunate to work with him on Pentium, and Xeon, and a few other things. But when we went to an executive committee to present Pentium... And by the way, internally, one of the names that... And makes sense here, descriptive, bunch of engineers, ProChip. "Hey, it's professional, it's premium, and it's chipped. So, it should be Prochip." So Andy had me give a presentation about the strengths of this thing, and he said, "Now, let me tell you why I think this is the right name." (01:09:56): He said, "Because I see the polarization here in it amongst people. There's this ProChip over here, there's the Pentium thing." He said, "That tells me there's energy for Pentium here." And he said, "That's why I think we should go with it." And I've never forgotten that. And so, we do look for that. And when we tell that story, people say, "You're right. There is... I mean, we are arguing about this, and there is an intensity with the name." And that's what you want. You don't want to go out in the marketplace, into this very competitive marketplace, regardless of the category, with something that doesn't have a level of boldness or intensity.
turns.zh: 对。而且顺便说，它的反面就是：我们寻找"两极分化"。我们寻找团队里为了这些事争得不可开交的那股张力，因为我们认为两极分化是这个词有力量的重要标志。有个有趣的故事，老实说，教会我这一点的人是 Andy Grove，关于 Pentium 这个名字，因为……我从他那儿学了很多。我总说，我很幸运能在 Pentium、Xeon 还有另外几个项目上和他共事。但当我们去执行委员会汇报 Pentium 时……顺便说，内部当时有个名字——放在这儿也说得通，一群工程师，描述性的，叫 ProChip。"嘿，它专业、高端、还是芯片，所以应该叫 ProChip。"所以 Andy 让我先讲了一遍这东西的优势，然后他说："现在，让我告诉你为什么我觉得这是对的名字。"（01:09:56）他说："因为我在这里看到了人们之间的两极分化。这边有个 ProChip，那边有个 Pentium。"他说："这告诉我，Pentium 这儿有能量。"他说："这就是我为什么觉得我们该用它。"我至今没忘。所以我们确实在找那个。当我们讲这个故事，人们会说："你说得对。确实……我是说，我们是在为这名字争论，而且这名字带着一股劲。"而这正是你想要的。你不想带着一个没有胆量、没有劲头的名字，进到这个竞争极其激烈的市场——不管什么品类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an amazing story. Just again, so kind of a tip here is if half of your team or, I don't know, some percent of your team hates it, some percent of your team loves it, that's a good sign.
turns.zh: 那故事太绝了。再说一遍，所以一个提示是：如果你团队里一半人、或者不管多少比例的人讨厌它，另一部分人爱它，那就是个好兆头。

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yeah, it is. It is. Look for that polarization. That's what we look for.
turns.zh: 对，是的。去找那种两极分化。那就是我们找的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also love this tip of asking people if, "Hey, our competitor just launched. They're called Windsurf." How your team reacts? If they're just like, "Oh, wow, that's a great name. I'm interested in that product." That's what you want to look for?
turns.zh: 我也很喜欢这个提示：去问大家"嘿，我们对手刚发布了，叫 Windsurf"。看你的团队什么反应？如果他们只是"哇，这名字真棒，我对那个产品感兴趣了"——这就是你要找的？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How important is the .com for the name you come up with? I imagine it's really hard to get these days. Just what do you think about domain name when you think about naming?
turns.zh: 你们想出来的名字，.com 有多重要？我想现在应该特别难拿到了。你考虑命名的时候，对域名是怎么看的？

turns.speaker: David Placek
turns.en: I am so glad you asked this question because at this point, it doesn't really matter at all. The .com or URL address has become an area code. And whether you're in 415 or 615, it doesn't really matter to people. And now with AI, SEO is going to be less important. And so, I just think the principle in play here is you got to get the right name first. And then if you can get the .com, sure, go ahead. But if you can't, there's ways around that. You can put a prefix in front of it or a little word in front of it or after it, or you go to .ai or something like that. But the principle in play is let's get the right name first.
